_meta.policy: Reference numbers only -- nothing in CI reads or diffs against this file. Manual comparison until S6 (Slang layout migration + perf-gate tooling); see spade/tests/bench/bench_core.cpp's and bench_sim.cpp's header comments for the full policy. Re-seed by hand (spade_bench --benchmark_format=json) when the comparison basis meaningfully changes (box, compiler, or a deliberate perf-affecting change worth re-baselining against) -- do not treat routine run-to-run noise as a reason to update this file.
_meta.seeded_by: Task 21 (close-out bench sweep, spade/s1-s4 plan): bench_sim.cpp added (BM_StepPlainBodies, BM_StepQuadWorlds), and BM_IntegrateOrientation re-measured alongside them in this same run (it could have been recorded alone via --benchmark_filter=BM_IntegrateOrientation; it was not, only because this run's purpose was seeding the two new benchmarks and re-measuring the existing one cost nothing extra). This box now has THREE recorded observations of BM_IntegrateOrientation's cpu_time: 27.9 ns (SDD ledger, S3 stage gate, 2026-08-09), 73.4375 ns (seeded at commit 76aa0d4, 2026-08-09), and 100.4 ns (this run, 2026-08-10) -- a >3.5x spread across three same-box, same-preset runs, which means this microbenchmark's run-to-run variance is too wide for its own recorded numbers to serve as a regression basis at this precision; see the bench spread-policy ticket (design-specs/kat-open-agendas.md's T21 section) rather than reading any pairwise delta here as a finding.
_meta.note: context/benchmarks below are the unmodified output of that command. world_substeps_per_sec is not a manual addition to this file -- it is a custom benchmark::Counter BM_StepQuadWorlds itself computes and emits as part of its normal --benchmark_format=json output (see bench_sim.cpp), so it is genuinely part of 'the output of that command', not an edit to it. This file is not hand-edited beyond adding this _meta block.
_meta.spec_comparison: engine design spec §12 rate-envelope targets (design-specs/kat-spade-engine-design.html; quoting closely, not claiming byte-for-byte verbatim -- the source is HTML markup, this is a transliteration of its text): 'single world >= 10 kHz substeps CPU for a quadrotor-class scene ... batched headless >= 64 worlds x 1 kHz faster than real time on the dev GPU. Misses trigger design review, not silent acceptance.' Both CPU-measurable targets are HIT on this run, on TWO timing bases. CPU-time basis (google-benchmark's default -- neither BM_StepQuadWorlds nor BM_StepPlainBodies calls ->UseRealTime(), so items_per_second/world_substeps_per_sec below are computed from cpu_time, not wall-clock real_time): BM_StepQuadWorlds/1's items_per_second (296,218 substeps/sec, single world, quad+IMU scene) clears the 10 kHz floor by ~30x; BM_StepQuadWorlds/64's world_substeps_per_sec (176,223 world-substeps/sec) clears the 64,000 (64 worlds x 1 kHz) floor by ~2.75x. That basis is the right one for the FIRST target (it says 'CPU substeps' explicitly) but the SECOND target's own phrasing -- 'faster than real time' -- is inherently a wall-clock claim, so the honest comparison recomputes on real_time instead: BM_StepQuadWorlds/1 clears the 10 kHz floor by ~28.6x (286,342 substeps/sec from real_time = 174,609.67 ns/iter), and BM_StepQuadWorlds/64 clears the 64,000 floor by ~2.80x (179,148 world-substeps/sec from real_time = 17,862,367.57 ns/iter) -- both targets HOLD on the wall-clock basis too, with a lower but still comfortable margin on the batched target. The spec phrases the batched target 'on the dev GPU' -- this run is the CPU reference twin (v2 has no GPU backend before S6), so it is a strong signal, not the literal target measurement; that one first becomes possible at S6. The third §12 target (viewport: 1 world + few vehicles, 1 kHz physics + 60 fps render concurrently) is not applicable to a headless bench with no renderer. BM_StepPlainBodies is not a §12 target scene (no vehicle, no IMU) -- it exists to show step-loop throughput scaling with body count alone; see bench_sim.cpp's header comment for why its three points are not directly comparable to each other (different dynamical regimes, not a regression signal). steps/sec == substeps/sec throughout this file: every Simulation is created with substeps = 1 (see bench_sim.cpp), so items_per_second is reported in substeps/sec directly and needs no conversion.
